title: Thomas More (1478–1535)
hook: Henry VIII's chancellor, beheaded for conscience, joking on the scaffold
carry: the king's good servant, god's first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc: a farm girl who led armies and was burned at nineteen. Your line was I am not afraid. Where did you stand by what you knew was right? Day ninety-one.

London, July 1535. A man climbs a scaffold on Tower Hill. He's been in the Tower for over a year, and he's thin and gray. The steps are shaky, so he turns to the officer beside him and says, more or less: help me up, and as for coming down, I'll manage that myself. He was famous for jokes like that. Not long ago this man was Lord Chancellor to King Henry the Eighth. He wrote Utopia. He was a friend of the king. And he's about to die because of one thing he would not say. Today, Thomas More.
screen: `TOWER HILL, JULY 1535.` → `A JOKE ON THE SCAFFOLD.` → `ONE THING HE WOULD NOT SAY.`

segments.voice: Thomas More was a London lawyer, a father of four, with a house full of books, children, animals and arguments. He gave his daughters the same serious education as a son, which was rare then. He loved the law, and he loved his king. Then Henry wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon ended, and the Pope wouldn't do it. So Henry broke with Rome and had himself declared head of the Church in England. More resigned as chancellor and went quiet. But in 1534 every leading subject was told to swear an oath that went with the king's new marriage and against the Pope's authority. More refused. And here's the clever, careful part: he refused silently. He never said why. More believed that under English law, silence could not be treated as treason, so he held his tongue and trusted the law he'd served all his life. It didn't save him. At his trial, a witness named Richard Rich testified to words More swore he never said. Only then, condemned, did More speak his mind about the Church. On the scaffold, the story goes, he said he died the king's good servant, but God's first. He didn't hate the king. He just knew the order. It's honest to add: as chancellor, More pursued Protestants hard, and some were burned in those years. Catholics honor him as a martyr of conscience, and historians still argue over that record. The Church canonized him in 1935, and Pope John Paul the Second named him patron of politicians.
screen: `A LAWYER, A FATHER, THE KING'S FRIEND.` · `THE OATH HE WOULDN'T SWEAR.` · `HE REFUSED IN SILENCE.` · `A MARTYR, AND A HARD RECORD.` · then, large: `THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, BUT GOD'S FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one quiet promise. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise you've made that nobody is checking. To call someone. To stop saying a certain thing. To be honest about something small. Pick one. You don't have to tell anyone, the way More didn't explain himself. Just hold it and decide to keep it. If you pray, you can ask Thomas More to pray for you, the way Catholics ask the saints. The bell holds the time.
Thomas More. Lawyer, father, chancellor, and a saint who died for what he would not swear, with a joke on his lips. Today's word.

Your line: the king's good servant, God's first. That ends a week of saints: Augustine, Patrick, Benedict and Scholastica, Clare, Catherine, Joan, and More. Today, serve someone well, and know what comes first. Day ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saints Thomas More and John Fisher on June 22; many lawyers attend a yearly 'Red Mass', and More is invoked as patron of statesmen and politicians.

fork.setup: you're Thomas More. the king demands you swear an oath you can't swear. what do you do?
options: swear it and keep your doubts to yourself.
refuse, and publicly condemn the king.
refuse, and say nothing about why.
fork.reveal: he refused and stayed silent, trusting the law that silence isn't treason. only a witness's testimony, which More said was false, condemned him.

original.note: Greek: no place. More built the name of his book Utopia from these two words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who defied a king.
what it means: a man who loved his king, refused one oath in silence, and died saying God came first.
what a scholar hears: the scaffold words come from a report written soon after his death, not from More's own pen, and his treatment of Protestants is still debated.

notes: 'The king's good servant, but God's first': reported in the Paris News Letter, a contemporary account; not More's own writing. Paraphrased, not quoted.
Scaffold joke ('see me safe up, and for my coming down let me shift for myself') is from Roper / early accounts; paraphrased. Confirm.
More's age at death (born 1478, died 6 July 1535, so 57) and 'second most powerful person in England' as Lord Chancellor: confirm phrasing.
The 1534 oath accompanied the Act of Succession; confirm the summary 'went with the king's new marriage and against the Pope's authority'.

Silence and treason: More relied on the legal maxim that silence gives consent / cannot be treason; confirm the simplification. Reviewer softened the voice to 'More believed that under English law...' because how far silence protected him is debated by legal historians.
More's pursuit of heretics as chancellor (several burnings 1530–1532) stated briefly and without ranking; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this honesty.
Canonized 1935 with John Fisher; feast June 22; named patron of statesmen and politicians by John Paul II in 2000. Confirm.
Word and carry kept exactly as in the index ('god's' lowercase in the carry field).
